sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar-2 les 14, over zinnen die met een bijzin beginnen.
sentences.en: Today we are practicing Dutch sentences, with the grammar from #dutchgrammar-2 lesson 14, about sentences that start with a subordinate clause.

sentences.nl: Martin is onderweg naar Drenthe.
sentences.en: Martin is on his way to Drenthe.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin is on-the-way to Drenthe.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Onderweg" is a compound word meaning "on the way" or "en route." It functions as an adverb here.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to" when indicating direction or destination.  
• Word order follows a typical subject-verb-object/adverbial structure.

Examples:  
• Zij is onderweg naar school. (She is on the way to school.)  
• Wij zijn onderweg naar een vergadering. (We are on the way to a meeting.)  
• De trein is onderweg naar Amsterdam. (The train is on the way to Amsterdam.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa is onderweg naar de supermarkt. (Lisa is on the way to the supermarket.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Drenthe is a province in the northeastern part of the Netherlands, known for its nature reserves and prehistoric sites like the Hunebedden (dolmen). It is a popular destination for outdoor activities like cycling and hiking.

sentences.nl: Omdat Marieke de laatste avond, waarschijnlijk bij de studenten wil zijn,, komt hij een dag eerder.
sentences.en: Because Marieke probably wants to be with the students on the last evening, he is coming a day earlier.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because Marieke the last evening, probably with the students wants to be, comes he a day earlier.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Omdat" (because) introduces a subordinate clause, which affects word order: the conjugated verb "wil" (wants) goes to the end of the clause.  
• "Waarschijnlijk" (probably) is an adverb affecting the likelihood of the action, commonly placed before the verb or subject.  
• "Komt hij" (comes he) is the main clause, where the subject follows the verb in Dutch, a typical word order for main clauses.

Examples:  
• Omdat ik morgen vrij ben, ga ik vandaag langer werken. (Because I am free tomorrow, I will work longer today.)  
• Waarschijnlijk gaat het morgen regenen. (Probably, it will rain tomorrow.)  
• Hij komt morgen op bezoek. (He is coming to visit tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Omdat het weekend is, blijven we thuis. (Because it's the weekend, we are staying home.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• "Bij de studenten willen zijn" could imply a social or community aspect common in Dutch student life, where being part of the group is valued.

sentences.nl: Hij hoopt, dat Marieke vanavond met hem naar het meertje wil gaan…, om samen romantisch naar de maan te kijken.
sentences.en: He hopes that Marieke wants to go to the little lake with him tonight to romantically watch the moon together.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He hopes, that Marieke this evening with him to the little lake wants to go…, to together romantically at the moon to look.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a subordinate clause introduced by "dat" (that), which requires the verb to be placed at the end of the clause ("wil gaan").  
• The use of "om...te" + infinitive ("om samen romantisch naar de maan te kijken") indicates purpose, similar to "in order to" in English.  
• Dutch often uses diminutives like "meertje" (little lake) to convey fondness or smallness.  
  
Examples:  
- Hij denkt dat zij morgen de trein neemt. (He thinks that she will take the train tomorrow.)  
- Zij gaat naar de winkel om brood te kopen. (She goes to the store to buy bread.)  
- We zitten bij het haardvuurtje. (We are sitting by the little fireplace.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij verwacht, dat Peter haar vanmiddag naar het station wil brengen. (She expects that Peter wants to take her to the station this afternoon.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The concept of going to a "meertje" (little lake) for a romantic evening is a common theme in Dutch culture, where natural landscapes are cherished for leisure and romantic activities.

sentences.nl: Maar…
sentences.en: But...

sentences.nl: Terwijl Martin naar Drenthe reist,, zit Marieke bij Gianluca.
sentences.en: While Martin travels to Drenthe, Marieke is with Gianluca.

sentences.nl: Omdat Gianluca Marieke wel leuk vindt,, heeft hij haar uitgenodigd.
sentences.en: Because Gianluca likes Marieke, he invited her.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because Gianluca Marieke indeed nice finds, has he her invited.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a subordinate clause introduced by "omdat" (because), which sends the verb to the end of the clause.  
• "Wel" is used to add emphasis, similar to "indeed" or "after all."  
• "Vindt" is the present tense of "vinden" (to find), indicating an opinion or feeling.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Omdat het regent, blijven we binnen." (Because it is raining, we stay inside.)  
  - "Hij vindt het boek wel interessant." (He does find the book interesting.)  
  - "Ze heeft hem al uitgenodigd." (She has already invited him.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Omdat Lisa de film niet wil zien, blijft ze thuis. (Because Lisa doesn't want to see the movie, she stays home.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, inviting someone usually implies a certain level of hospitality and commitment. It can also be an indication of interest or friendship.

sentences.nl: Of Marieke Gianluca ook leuk vindt, weten we nog niet.
sentences.en: We don't know yet if Marieke also likes Gianluca.

sentences.nl: Zij heeft de uitnodiging wel geaccepteerd.
sentences.en: She did accept the invitation.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She has the invitation indeed accepted.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the present perfect tense ("heeft geaccepteerd"), which is common in Dutch to indicate an action that has been completed.  
• "Wel" adds emphasis or contrast, implying that the acceptance might be unexpected.  
• Word order in the main clause is Subject (Zij) + Auxiliary Verb (heeft) + Object (de uitnodiging) + Adverb (wel) + Past Participle (geaccepteerd).

Examples:  
• Hij heeft het project wel afgerond. (He did indeed complete the project.)  
• Ze heeft de film wel gezien. (She has indeed seen the movie.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij hebben het boek wel gelezen. (We have indeed read the book.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, accepting or declining an invitation often comes with a clear indication of commitment or reason, hence the emphasis with "wel" to confirm acceptance.

sentences.nl: Gianluca heeft voor Marieke gekookt.
sentences.en: Gianluca cooked for Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gianluca has for Marieke cooked.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the perfect tense, formed with the auxiliary verb "heeft" (has) and the past participle "gekookt" (cooked).  
• The preposition "voor" means "for" and indicates the beneficiary of the action.  
• The past participle "gekookt" comes at the end of the sentence, which is a typical Dutch word order for perfect tense sentences.

Examples:  
– Zij heeft voor mij een cadeautje gekocht. (She has bought a gift for me.)  
– Jullie hebben voor de kinderen gezorgd. (You have taken care of the children.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa heeft voor haar vrienden een taart gebakken. (Lisa has baked a cake for her friends.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, cooking for someone is often seen as a gesture of care and hospitality. It's common for friends and family to gather for meals at home.

sentences.nl: Hij heeft gezegd dat hij goed pizza’s kan maken.
sentences.en: He said that he can make good pizzas.

sentences.nl: Hoewel Marieke eigenlijk van Hollandse kost houdt,, vindt ze pizza ook wel lekker.
sentences.en: Although Marieke actually likes Dutch food, she also finds pizza quite tasty.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Although Marieke actually of Dutch food loves, finds she pizza also indeed tasty.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hoewel" (although) is a subordinating conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, affecting word order.  
• "Eigenlijk" (actually) is an adverb that modifies "houdt van" (loves). The phrase "houden van" means "to love" or "to like" something.  
• "Hollandse kost" refers to traditional Dutch food, a fixed phrase.  
• "Vindt ze pizza ook wel lekker" follows the structure of subject-verb inversion after a subordinating clause.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Hoewel het regent, gaan we toch naar buiten." (Although it is raining, we are going outside anyway.)  
  - "Ik hou eigenlijk van lezen." (I actually love reading.)  
  - "Zij vindt soep ook wel lekker." (She finds soup also indeed tasty.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hoewel hij normaal gesproken geen koffie drinkt, heeft hij vandaag een kopje gehad. (Although he normally doesn't drink coffee, he had a cup today.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Hollandse kost" usually refers to traditional Dutch meals, which often include potatoes, meat, and vegetables. This type of food is considered hearty and simple, reflecting the agrarian history of the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Voordat hij het eten op tafel zet,, vraagt hij: ‘Heb je zin in een glaasje wijn?’
sentences.en: Before he sets the food on the table, he asks, 'Do you feel like a glass of wine?'
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Before he the food on table puts, asks he: 'Have you desire in a glass wine?'

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Voordat" is a subordinating conjunction, which sends the verb to the end of the clause.  
• "Zet" is the third person singular present tense of "zetten" (to put/set).  
• "Heb je zin in" is an idiomatic expression meaning "Do you feel like" or "Do you fancy."  
• Examples:  
  - "Voordat ik ga slapen, lees ik een boek." (Before I go to sleep, I read a book.)  
  - "Heb je zin in een wandeling?" (Do you feel like a walk?)  
  - "Hij vraagt of je mee wilt gaan." (He asks if you want to come along.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Voordat zij de deur opendoet, kijkt ze door het raam. (Before she opens the door, she looks through the window.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

sentences.nl: Ondanks dat ik dat wel wil,, kan ik beter een glaasje water nemen.
sentences.en: Even though I want to, I better have a glass of water.

sentences.nl: De docenten mogen alleen alcohol, op de laatste avond!
sentences.en: The teachers are only allowed alcohol on the last evening!

sentences.en: One little drink can't hurt, can it? — And it's almost the last evening.

sentences.nl: Eh… OK vooruit.
sentences.en: Eh… OK fine.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Eh… OK forward.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Eh" is an interjection used to express hesitation or thinking.  
• "OK" is borrowed from English, used to express agreement.  
• "Vooruit" literally means "forward," but in this context, it is an idiomatic expression meaning "all right" or "let's go ahead."  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Vooruit dan maar." (All right then.)  
  - "Hij loopt vooruit." (He walks ahead.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Vooruit, ik zal het doen." (All right, I will do it.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, using "vooruit" in this context often indicates a mild reluctance being overcome, leading to agreement or compliance with a suggestion or request.

sentences.nl: Als Bart het niet ziet, dan kan het wel.
sentences.en: If Bart doesn't see it, then it's fine.

sentences.nl: Nou proost!
sentences.en: Well, cheers!

sentences.nl: Dan haalt Gianluca de pizza.
sentences.en: Then Gianluca picks up the pizza.

sentences.nl: Op de pizza heeft hij een hartje getekend…
sentences.en: He drew a heart on the pizza...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• On the pizza has he a heart drawn…

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses inversion, which is common in Dutch when a sentence begins with something other than the subject. Here, "Op de pizza" starts the sentence, so the verb "heeft" comes before the subject "hij."  
• The verb "getekend" is the past participle of "tekenen" (to draw), used with "heeft" to form the present perfect tense.  
• Example 1: "Op de muur heeft zij een schilderij gehangen." (On the wall, she has hung a painting.)  
• Example 2: "In de tuin hebben we bloemen geplant." (In the garden, we have planted flowers.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Op het strand heeft zij een zandkasteel gebouwd." (On the beach, she has built a sandcastle.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Drawing shapes like hearts on pizzas or other foods can be seen as a playful or romantic gesture, often done during special occasions or dates in the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: En je raadt het al…
sentences.en: And you guessed it...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And you guess it already...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En" is a conjunction meaning "and."  
• "Je" is an informal singular pronoun meaning "you."  
• "Raadt" is the second-person singular present tense of the verb "raden," meaning "to guess."  
• "Het" is a pronoun meaning "it."  
• "Al" is an adverb meaning "already." It indicates that the action is expected or anticipated.  
• The structure "je raadt het al" is often used to suggest that something is obvious or predictable.

• Examples:  
  - "Ik denk dat je het al weet." (I think you already know it.)  
  - "En je ziet het al gebeuren." (And you see it happening already.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "En je weet het al... het gaat regenen." (And you already know it... it's going to rain.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This phrase is often used in storytelling or conversation to create a connection with the listener, suggesting that what follows is predictable or a common experience.

sentences.nl: Marieke moet blozen!
sentences.en: Marieke has to blush!

sentences.nl: Net op dat moment komt Xing voorbij…
sentences.en: Just at that moment, Xing passes by…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Just at that moment comes Xing by...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Net op dat moment" means "just at that moment," where "net" indicates precision in timing.  
• "Komt voorbij" is in the present tense, indicating an action happening right now. "Voorbij" means "by" or "past," used to indicate movement.  
• Example 1: "Net op tijd was hij klaar." (Just in time he was ready.)  
• Example 2: "Ze komt elke dag voorbij." (She comes by every day.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Net op dat moment ging de telefoon." (Just at that moment, the phone rang.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch storytelling or conversation, specifying timing with expressions like "Net op dat moment" adds a dramatic or emphatic effect, common in both spoken and written narratives.

sentences.nl: Doordat ze Gianluca en Marieke, romantisch ziet eten,, met een glaasje wijn en een pizza met een hartje,, trekt ze de conclusie:, Hmmm… arme Martin…
sentences.en: Seeing Gianluca and Marieke having a romantic meal, with a glass of wine and a heart-shaped pizza, she concludes: Hmmm… poor Martin…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because she Gianluca and Marieke romantically sees eating, with a little glass of wine and a pizza with a little heart, draws she the conclusion: Hmmm… poor Martin…

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Doordat" is a subordinating conjunction meaning "because" or "due to," and it introduces a subordinate clause.  
• The verb "ziet" (sees) is in the present tense. In Dutch, verbs often come second in the sentence, but in subordinate clauses, the verb goes to the end.  
• "Trekt ze de conclusie" translates to "draws the conclusion." In Dutch, "de conclusie trekken" is a common expression.  

Examples:  
– "Doordat het regent, blijven we binnen." (Because it rains, we stay inside.)  
– "Ze trekt de conclusie dat hij gelijk heeft." (She concludes that he is right.)  
– "Met een glimlach zegt hij dag." (With a smile, he says goodbye.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Doordat de kinderen spelen, is het huis een rommel." (Because the children are playing, the house is a mess.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, dining with wine and pizza is often seen as a casual yet romantic gesture, reflecting a European influence on casual dining habits.

sentences.nl: Ze loopt snel verder.
sentences.en: She walks quickly onward.

sentences.nl: Maar inmiddels is Martin ook op het vakantiepark.
sentences.en: But by now Martin is also at the holiday park.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But meanwhile is Martin also at the holiday park.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Inmiddels" means "meanwhile" or "by now," indicating a progression of time.  
• The word order "is Martin ook" follows the subject-verb-object structure typical in Dutch main clauses.  
• "Op het vakantiepark" uses the preposition "op" (at/on) for location, which is common when referring to being at a place.

Examples:  
• Inmiddels heeft hij geleerd te zwemmen. (Meanwhile, he has learned to swim.)  
• Ze is inmiddels een expert geworden. (She has become an expert by now.)  
• We zijn op het station. (We are at the station.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Inmiddels is de trein ook aangekomen. (By now, the train has also arrived.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Vacation parks are a popular holiday choice in the Netherlands, often featuring amenities like swimming pools, restaurants, and activities for families.

sentences.nl: Hij staat bij de receptie.
sentences.en: He is at the reception.

sentences.nl: Wanneer hij naar de Summer School wil lopen, ziet hij Xing.
sentences.en: When he wants to walk to the Summer School, he sees Xing.

sentences.nl: Hoi Xing.
sentences.en: Hi Xing.

sentences.nl: Oh… hoi Martin…
sentences.en: Oh… hi Martin…

sentences.nl: Eh… hoe gaat het met jou? — Goed.
sentences.en: Uh... how are you? — Good.

sentences.nl: Ik kom voor Marieke.
sentences.en: I'm here for Marieke.

sentences.nl: Eh… oh… eh… Martin…
sentences.en: Eh... oh... eh... Martin...

sentences.nl: Xing raakt een beetje in paniek.
sentences.en: Xing is getting a bit panicked.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing gets a bit in panic.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Raakt" is the present tense form of "raken," meaning "to get" or "to become" in this context.  
• "Een beetje" translates to "a bit" or "a little," used to modify the extent of the action.  
• "In paniek" means "in panic," where "in" is a preposition used with states or conditions.

• Examples:  
  - Hij raakt vaak in de war. (He often gets confused.)  
  - Zij raakt snel in slaap. (She falls asleep quickly.)  
  - Ik raakte in de problemen. (I got into trouble.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maria raakt een beetje geïrriteerd. (Maria gets a bit irritated.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Ze is bang dat Martin straks Marieke met Gianluca ziet.
sentences.en: She is afraid that Martin will soon see Marieke with Gianluca.

sentences.nl: Omdat ze dat wil voorkomen, bedenkt ze een smoesje.
sentences.en: Because she wants to prevent that, she makes up an excuse.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because she that wants to prevent, invents she an excuse.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinating Conjunction "omdat":** This word introduces a subordinate clause, which causes the verb to move to the end of the clause.  
• **Verb Placement:** In subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb ("wil") is placed at the end. In the main clause ("bedenkt ze een smoesje"), the subject ("ze") follows the verb ("bedenkt").  
• **Vocabulary:** "Voorkomen" means "to prevent," and "smoesje" is a diminutive form of "smoes," meaning "excuse" or "pretext."

Extra Examples:  
- Omdat het regent, nemen we een paraplu mee. (Because it is raining, we take an umbrella with us.)  
- Ze wil voorkomen dat het weer gebeurt. (She wants to prevent it from happening again.)  
- Hij bedenkt vaak smoesjes om niet te hoeven gaan. (He often comes up with excuses to not have to go.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Omdat hij de trein miste, kwam hij te laat aan. (Because he missed the train, he arrived late.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, being direct and straightforward is valued, but it's also common to use "smoesjes" or little excuses to politely avoid situations or commitments.

sentences.nl: Martin, kom even met me mee.
sentences.en: Martin, come with me for a moment.

sentences.nl: Aangezien je met Marieke naar het bruggetje wil,, kan ik jou alvast laten zien waar het is.
sentences.en: Since you want to go to the little bridge with Marieke, I can already show you where it is.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Since you with Marieke to the little bridge want, can I you already let see where it is.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Aangezien" is a conjunction meaning "since" or "because," introducing a reason or cause.  
• The word order "je met Marieke naar het bruggetje wil" places the verb "wil" (want) at the end of the clause, which is typical in subordinate clauses.  
• "Alvast" means "already" or "in advance," indicating doing something beforehand.

Extra phrases:  
- "Aangezien het regent, blijven we binnen." (Since it is raining, we stay inside.)  
- "Ik kan jou alvast helpen met je huiswerk." (I can already help you with your homework.)  
- "Hij liet me zien waar het station is." (He let me see where the station is.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Aangezien hij morgen vertrekt, moeten we nu afscheid nemen. (Since he leaves tomorrow, we must say goodbye now.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives like "bruggetje" (little bridge) is common in Dutch to add a sense of endearment or smallness.

sentences.nl: Oh… Xing, dat is heel aardig van je.
sentences.en: Oh… Xing, that is very kind of you.

sentences.nl: Doei!
sentences.en: Bye!

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

die.spelling: In Dutch, the pronoun 'die' is pronounced with a long /i/ sound, which is common for pronouns and demonstratives.
die.fast: In connected speech, 'die' may become a reduced vowel sound, especially in fast speech or informal contexts.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

wil.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ in wil closes with the liquid /l/.
wil.fast: In fast speech, ‘wil ik’ may blend, reducing the /l/ to a lighter touch before the vowel.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.
